Leukemia

Case-Based Learning · Haematology
Case 1 of 5
The Pale, Bruising Child
Paediatric Acute Leukaemia ALL

A 5-year-old boy is brought to the paediatric OPD with complaints of fever for two weeks, fatigue, and decreased appetite. His mother noticed that he bruises easily and has frequent nosebleeds.

On examination, he appears pale and has cervical lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly.

Clinical Questions
1. What is the most likely diagnosis in this child?
2. What investigations would you order in this child?
Model Answer First-line investigations:
• FBC with differential — characteristically shows anaemia, thrombocytopenia, and variable WBC (may be low, normal, or markedly elevated)
• Peripheral blood smear — to identify lymphoblasts
• Bone marrow aspiration/trephine — definitive; ≥20% blasts confirms acute leukaemia

Additional workup:
• Immunophenotyping (flow cytometry) — distinguishes B-ALL from T-ALL
• Cytogenetics / FISH — identifies prognostic translocations (e.g. t(12;21) TEL-AML1 = good prognosis; t(9;22) Philadelphia = poor prognosis)
• LDH, uric acid — assess tumour burden
• Renal and liver function, coagulation screen
• CXR / CT chest — assess for mediastinal mass (T-ALL)
3. Which peripheral smear finding is most characteristic of ALL?
4. What are the classic bone marrow aspiration findings in ALL?
Model Answer • Hypercellular marrow with replacement of normal haematopoietic elements
• ≥20% lymphoblasts (WHO criterion for acute leukaemia)
• Blasts are small-to-medium with high N:C ratio, fine ("dusty") chromatin, inconspicuous nucleoli, no Auer rods
• Normal erythroid and myeloid precursors markedly suppressed
• Confirmed by immunophenotyping: TdT+, CD10+, CD19+ (B-ALL); CD3+, CD7+ (T-ALL)
Case 2 of 5
The Bleeding Farmer
Adult AML APL — M3 DIC

A 40-year-old male farmer presents with sudden-onset fatigue, gum bleeding, and high-grade fever for one week. No significant past medical history.

On examination: pallor, petechiae, mild splenomegaly.

Laboratory Findings
Haemoglobin7.2 g/dL
WBC45,000/mm³
Platelets30,000/mm³
Peripheral smearBlasts present
Figure (B) — Peripheral blood smear. Identify the structures indicated by the arrows.
Clinical Questions
1. What structures are shown by the arrows in the smear image, and what do they indicate?
Model Answer The arrows point to Auer rods — elongated, needle-like cytoplasmic inclusions formed from fused primary (azurophilic) granules.

Significance:
• Pathognomonic of myeloid leukaemia (AML); never seen in ALL or CLL
• Their presence immediately excludes lymphoid malignancy
• In APL (AML-M3), blasts may contain bundles of Auer rods called "faggot cells"
• Positive MPO (myeloperoxidase) staining confirms myeloid lineage
2. How would you differentiate AML from other acute leukaemias?
Model Answer Morphology: Auer rods, larger blasts, more cytoplasm in AML vs. scant cytoplasm in ALL

Cytochemistry:
• MPO / Sudan Black B — positive in AML, negative in ALL
• PAS — strongly positive in ALL (block positivity)

Immunophenotyping (flow cytometry):
• AML: CD13, CD33, CD117, MPO
• B-ALL: CD10, CD19, CD22, TdT
• T-ALL: CD3, CD7, TdT

Genetics:
• t(15;17) PML-RARA → APL (AML-M3)
• t(8;21), inv(16) → good-prognosis AML subtypes
Day 3 of Treatment

Genetic testing confirmed t(15;17) PML-RARA positive → Acute Promyelocytic Leukaemia (APL). Induction with ATRA and arsenic trioxide was commenced.

On Day 3, the patient develops sudden oozing from venipuncture sites, haematuria, gum bleeding, worsening dyspnoea, and mild confusion. BP 90/60 mmHg, HR 110/min.

Repeat Investigations
PTProlonged
aPTTProlonged
Platelets14,000/mm³
Fibrinogen95 mg/dL (↓)
D-dimerMarkedly ↑
LDHElevated
Blood smearPersistent promyelocytes
3. What complication has developed, and why does it occur specifically in APL?
Explanation DIC is the correct answer. APL (AML-M3) blasts release granule contents rich in tissue factor and proteolytic enzymes, triggering systemic activation of both the coagulation and fibrinolytic cascades → consumption of clotting factors, fibrinogen, and platelets → widespread bleeding.

Key lab pattern of DIC: prolonged PT/aPTT + low fibrinogen + low platelets + elevated D-dimer (fibrin degradation products).

Management: FFP, cryoprecipitate, platelet transfusion + urgent continuation of ATRA (which promotes differentiation and reduces promyelocyte granule release).
Case 3 of 5
The Young Woman with Pancytopaenia
Young Adult Pancytopaenia Aplastic Anaemia

A 19-year-old female presents with increasing fatigue, frequent headaches, dizziness, easy bruising, gum bleeding, low-grade fever, and sore throat over the past month.

On examination: pallor, scattered petechiae over lower limbs, mild tachycardia. No lymphadenopathy or organomegaly.

Clinical Questions
1. What are your top differential diagnoses for this presentation?
Differentials 1. Aplastic anaemia — primary concern given pancytopaenia without organomegaly
2. Acute leukaemia (ALL/AML) — must rule out with bone marrow exam
3. Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) — less common in young patients
4. Nutritional deficiency (B12/folate) — can cause pancytopaenia but unlikely with petechiae
5. Viral bone marrow suppression — EBV, CMV, Parvovirus B19, HIV
6. SLE — can cause immune-mediated pancytopaenia in young women
2. What investigations would you order?
Investigations Blood tests: FBC with differential, reticulocyte count, peripheral smear
Serology: EBV, CMV, Parvovirus B19, HIV, hepatitis panel
Autoimmune screen: ANA, dsDNA (exclude SLE)
Bone marrow aspiration + trephine biopsy — essential to characterise cellularity and exclude leukaemia/MDS
B12, folate, iron studies
Renal and liver function, coagulation screen
Flow cytometry (PNH screen) — paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria can co-exist with aplastic anaemia
Investigation Results
Haemoglobin6.8 g/dL
WBC2,200/mm³
Neutrophils800/mm³
Platelets18,000/mm³
ReticulocytesLow
SerologyNegative
Peripheral smearNormocytic normochromic; reduced elements; no blasts
Bone marrowHypocellular; fatty replacement
3. What is the most likely diagnosis, and how would you classify its severity?
4. How does aplastic anaemia differ from acute leukaemia on bone marrow biopsy?
Comparison
FeatureAplastic AnaemiaAcute Leukaemia
Marrow cellularity↓ Hypocellular↑ Hypercellular
Blast cellsAbsent≥20% (WHO criterion)
Fat replacementProminentMinimal
Normal precursorsMarkedly reducedReplaced by blasts
Case 4 of 5
The Incidental Leucocytosis
Middle-aged Adult CML Philadelphia Chromosome

A 55-year-old man attends for a routine check-up and is incidentally found to have a WBC count of 120,000/mm³. He reports only mild fatigue. On examination, there is moderate splenomegaly. Peripheral smear shows increased granulocytes at all stages of maturation.

Peripheral blood smear — note the spectrum of granulocyte maturation: myeloblasts, promyelocytes, myelocytes, metamyelocytes, band forms, and segmented neutrophils.
Clinical Questions
1. What investigations confirm the diagnosis of CML?
Model Answer Peripheral smear: Entire granulocyte spectrum (myeloblasts → mature neutrophils), basophilia, eosinophilia, thrombocytosis (early)

Bone marrow: Hypercellular with myeloid hyperplasia; M:E ratio ↑↑

Cytogenetics:
• Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22) on conventional karyotyping — diagnostic
• BCR-ABL1 fusion gene by FISH or RT-PCR — highly sensitive, monitors response to therapy

Other:
• Leukocyte alkaline phosphatase (LAP) score — markedly decreased in CML (helps distinguish from leukaemoid reaction)
• Elevated B12, uric acid, LDH
2. What is the significance of the Philadelphia chromosome?
3. How is CML staged, and what marks the transition to blast crisis?
Model Answer Chronic phase (years): <10% blasts in blood/marrow; mild symptoms; splenomegaly. Responds well to TKIs (imatinib/dasatinib).

Accelerated phase: 10–19% blasts; increasing basophils (>20%); progressive cytogenetic evolution; worsening cytopaenias; splenomegaly despite therapy.

Blast crisis (blast phase): ≥20% blasts (myeloid or lymphoid) — functionally resembles AML or ALL. Median survival ~3–6 months without allogeneic SCT.

Triggers of transformation: Additional chromosomal abnormalities, BCR-ABL kinase domain mutations (especially T315I — "gatekeeper" mutation).
Case 5 of 5
The Jaundiced CLL Patient
Elderly CLL AIHA Richter Transformation

A 72-year-old man with known CLL diagnosed 3 years ago (previously under watchful waiting) presents with increasing fatigue, dyspnoea on exertion, jaundice, low-grade fever, and 4 kg unintentional weight loss over 2 months.

On examination: pallor, mild icterus, cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy, mild splenomegaly.

Laboratory Results
Haemoglobin6.5 g/dL
Reticulocytes8% (↑)
Total bilirubin3.4 mg/dL
Direct bilirubin0.7 mg/dL
LDHElevated
HaptoglobinLow
Direct Coombs (DAT)Positive
WBC85,000/mm³ (85% lymphocytes)
Peripheral smearSpherocytes + smudge cells
Peripheral blood smear (CLL) — note the abundant small mature lymphocytes and scattered smudge cells (fragile CLL cells ruptured during smear preparation). Spherocytes indicate coexisting AIHA.
Clinical Questions
1. What are the possible causes of anaemia in a patient with CLL?
Causes of Anaemia in CLL 1. Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (AIHA) — most common immune complication; CLL B-cells produce warm IgG autoantibodies against RBCs (as in this case)

2. Bone marrow infiltration — CLL cells crowd out erythroid precursors → hypoproliferative anaemia

3. Hypersplenism — increased RBC sequestration and destruction in an enlarged spleen

4. Chemotherapy-induced myelosuppression — if the patient has been treated

5. Pure red cell aplasia (PRCA) — rare autoimmune suppression of erythropoiesis

6. Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) can co-occur (Evans syndrome = AIHA + ITP)
2. Which finding is most consistent with autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (AIHA) in this patient?
3. How do you interpret the significance of the positive Direct Antiglobulin Test (DAT/Coombs) in this context?
Model Answer The positive DAT confirms that IgG autoantibodies (and/or complement C3d) are bound to the surface of the patient's own red blood cells — the hallmark of warm AIHA.

Why does this happen in CLL?
Malignant CLL B-cells produce dysfunctional autoantibodies that cross-react with RBC surface antigens (commonly Rh system). This is an immune dysregulation specific to the disease, not a drug effect.

Clinical significance:
• AIHA develops in ~10–25% of CLL patients during the disease course
• Its onset often signals disease progression or a need to start/change therapy
• Treatment: steroids (prednisolone) first-line; rituximab, cyclosporine, or CLL-directed therapy if refractory
• A positive DAT alone without haemolysis does not require treatment — clinical correlation is essential
4. The patient develops rapidly enlarging cervical nodes and his LDH triples over 2 weeks. What complication should you suspect?
